title: Poisson log-linear models
dek: Y ~ Poisson(μ), log μ = xᵀβ + offset. The likelihood is ∑ (y log μ − μ). Mean equals variance until the data laugh.
story: Counts — colony-forming units, incident cases, variant reads — often start as Poisson. The log link keeps μ > 0. With an offset log(t), β on a covariate is a log rate ratio: μ = t e^{xᵀβ}.
The log-likelihood ℓ(β) = ∑ (yᵢ xᵢᵀβ − exp(xᵢᵀβ + oᵢ)) up to a factorial constant. Score Xᵀ(y − μ) = 0: again the exponential-family mean match. IRLS weights are W = μ for the canonical log link.

The Poisson variance V(μ) = μ is the fragile part. TB cluster sizes, weekly notifications, and RNA-seq counts are usually overdispersed. Quasi-Poisson, negative binomial, or a hierarchical Poisson are the three adult forks — not “the Poisson p-value was 10⁻¹² so it must be real.”
deepTitle: Offsets, zeros, and the likelihood you actually want
deep: Offset discipline: person-time, culture-days, or sequencing depth belong in oᵢ = log tᵢ unless you have a reason to estimate a coefficient on log t (testing whether the rate scales linearly with exposure).

Many zeros: a Poisson with small μ can produce zeros honestly. Excess zeros from a mixture (no risk vs some risk) want a zero-inflated or hurdle likelihood. Those are not nested in a plain Poisson without a mixture parameter on the boundary.
Rate vs count: if tᵢ varies, modelling Y without an offset compares expected counts, not rates. A large district will dominate and you will rediscover population size.

Contingency tables with Poisson log-linear models are multinomial in disguise after conditioning on margins. Independence is a nested restriction on interaction terms — an LRT with a χ²_df that is the usual Pearson test’s likelihood cousin.

formulas.label: Poisson log-likelihood (canonical log)
formulas.expression: ℓ(β) = ∑ᵢ [ yᵢ ηᵢ − e^{ηᵢ} ],   ηᵢ = xᵢᵀβ + oᵢ
formulas.note: Drop ∑ log(yᵢ!); it does not depend on β.

formulas.label: Rate form
formulas.note: offset oᵢ = log tᵢ. exp(β_k) is a rate ratio.

visual.caption: Poisson GLM with exposure: tᵢ is observed, log tᵢ is a deterministic offset, μᵢ = exp(xᵢᵀβ + log tᵢ), and yᵢ is the count. Forgetting tᵢ puts population size into β.

example.title: Incident TB versus person-years
example.setup: Two districts: 12 cases in 4000 person-years, 18 cases in 3000 person-years. Log-linear Poisson with a district dummy and offset log(PY).

steps.title: Rates
steps.body: District A: 12/4000 = 0.003 per PY. District B: 18/3000 = 0.006 per PY. Crude rate ratio = 2.

steps.title: MLE
steps.body: With only a dummy and an offset, the MLE of the rate ratio is the crude ratio 2. The Poisson likelihood will also claim se from V = μ. If cases cluster in time, that se is too small.

steps.title: Without offset
steps.body: A model for raw counts would compare 12 vs 18 and discover that B is larger in counts while missing that A had more person-time. That is a different scientific question.

example.takeaway: Put exposure in the offset if the target is a rate. Then worry about V(μ) = μ.

check.prompt: An offset log(t) in a log-linear Poisson model is used to:
choices: Estimate a coefficient on t freely
Force the mean to scale with exposure t so that β lives on a rate scale
Turn the Poisson into a Gaussian
check.answer: Force the mean to scale with exposure t so that β lives on a rate scale
check.why: The coefficient on log t is frozen at 1. Overdispersion is a separate issue.

whyWrong.Estimate a coefficient on t freely: That would be a covariate, not an offset.

check.prompt: Canonical log Poisson, μ = 4. IRLS weight W = μ equals:
check.why: For canonical log, W = μ. Mean 4, weight 4.

check.prompt: On the Poisson plate, tᵢ is an observed node feeding the deterministic ηᵢ. That drawing says:
check.figureHint: tᵢ and xᵢ both arrow into ηᵢ.
choices: Exposure is a random effect with its own variance
Known exposure enters the linear predictor as an offset, not as a latent parameter
check.answer: Known exposure enters the linear predictor as an offset, not as a latent parameter
check.why: Filled node: observed. Diamond η: deterministic function of x, β, and log t.

whyWrong.Exposure is a random effect with its own: That would be an empty circle with a distribution.
